To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) MCF is able to identify cancer-specific metabolic pathway compositions from gene expression data; and that 2) these pathway compositions can be used to enhance cancer survival prediction.

(i) aggregating gene expression through metabolic pathways fails to predict cancer vs. non-cancerous samples; (ii) MCF identifies new cancer-mediated metabolic pathways; and (iii) MCF pathways are more informative than canonical pathways in predicting survival of breast cancer patients.
we have developed a data-driven method to infer new metabolic pathways that better predict cancer patient survival than standard classifiers based on canonical metabolic pathways.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel methods for integrating high-throughput gene expression measurements into metabolic networks in order to identify cancer-specific metabolic pathways.
the question how to aggregate gene expression measurements into pathways to enhance classification of cancerous vs. non-cancerous tissues and prediction of cancer patient outcome.
the development of a data-driven method for inferring cancer-associated metabolic pathways and their integration into a survival prediction framework for cancer patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the MCF method is able to generate new composite metabolic pathways from the human metabolic network that can be used to enhance cancer classification and survival prediction.
the MCF approach is a promising tool for the identification of metabolic pathway compositions that are altered during tumorigenesis and can be used to improve the diagnosis and prognosis of patients.
MCF pathways are more predictive than the canonical pathways, which is not surprising given that MCF pathways have been trained to be predictive.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the MCF approach can be a useful tool to discover metabolic alterations in cancer, and to predict cancer patients’ survival, and thus it can help in the diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis of cancer.
the MCF approach can be used to infer metabolic pathways associated with specific cancer types, which can then be used as a basis for building robust classifiers for cancer detection and prognosis.
data-driven pathway compositions are better than canonical pathways in predicting cancer vs normal samples and cancer survival.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the metabolic alterations in cancer are not captured by the canonical human metabolic pathway compositions.

the metabolic reorganization occurring in cancer can be effectively captured by integrating gene expression into a human metabolic model to generate novel pathway compositions that are more informative of cancer status and survival than canonical metabolic pathways.
the metabolic alterations that occur in cancer rewire metabolism through unconventional pathways, which can be identified via data-driven methods.
